title: Rules Versus Standards: An Economic Analysis
author: Louis Kaplow
version: Duke Law Journal 42:557, 1992, as published at the Duke repository

record.source: The cost analysis of the choice between a rule and a standard. Read for the reason a judgement is sometimes cheaper than a check, which is the question every instruction answers about itself.
record.kept: The asymmetry: a rule is expensive to make and cheap to apply, a standard is cheap to make and expensive to apply, and the choice turns on how often the situation recurs and how much is at stake each time.
record.rewritten: Stated as an authoring decision: the more often a situation recurs and the higher the cost of a wrong call, the more a gate earns the cost of being written. A judgement is the right form for the situation that occurs once.
record.added: The observer as the measure of the cost. A gate's price in this repository is a lint entry, a test and the upkeep the gate census measures, so the rule side of the trade is priced here rather than in the abstract.
record.dropped: The formal model, its welfare analysis and its treatment of adjudication costs, none of which changes the authoring decision.
